title: Notch: Signaling by Contact and by Cutting

generated.pipeline: extract → Gemini draft → Claude Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: What happens to a fruit fly embryo that has no working copy of the Notch gene?
cards.back: It builds too much nervous system and too little skin.
cards.why: In the embryo's outer layer, cells choose between nerve precursor and skin; without Notch, far too many cells choose nerve.
cards.quote: An embryo with no working copy builds too much nervous system and too little skin.

cards.front: Fruit fly Notch and the worm cell-fate gene {{c1::lin-12}} encode one family of single-pass membrane receptors.
cards.quote: Fly Notch and the worm cell-fate gene lin-12 encode one family of single-pass membrane receptors

cards.front: During embryonic nerve-versus-skin fate choice, why is Notch described as telling a cell "not you" rather than making a nerve cell?
cards.back: Notch suppresses the nerve-precursor fate so the receiving cell becomes skin instead; without Notch, far too many cells become nerve.
cards.quote: In the embryo's outer layer, each cell chooses between nerve precursor and skin; without Notch, far too many choose nerve.

cards.front: Notch's membrane-bound ligands are Delta and Serrate in fruit flies, and the Delta-like and {{c1::Jagged}} proteins in mammals.
cards.quote: Notch's ligands are single-pass membrane proteins fixed in the sending cell: Delta and Serrate in flies, and the Delta-like and Jagged proteins in mammals.
cards.section: Touch, pull and the lock

cards.front: Why does standard Notch signaling in flies and mammals occur mainly between cells that touch?
cards.back: Both Notch and its ligands are single-pass membrane proteins fixed in opposing cells, so they interact only where cell surfaces meet.
cards.why: Exceptions are a few secreted worm ligands and cells contacting neighbors several diameters away via thin extensions.
cards.quote: Because Notch is anchored in the receiving cell, the main fly and mammalian pathways signal only where cells touch
cards.section: Touch, pull and the lock

cards.front: Just outside the receiving cell membrane, three small modules on Notch fold into a lock—the {{c1::negative regulatory region}}—that hides the cutting site.
cards.quote: three small modules fold into a lock—the negative regulatory region—that hides Notch's cutting site.
cards.section: Touch, pull and the lock

cards.front: In the standard account of Notch activation, the sending cell pulls bound ligand inward by {{c1::endocytosis}}, pinching membrane in to form a vesicle.
cards.quote: the sending cell pulls bound ligand inward by endocytosis (the pinching-in of membrane to form a vesicle)
cards.section: Touch, pull and the lock

cards.front: In the standard account of Notch signaling, why does ligand binding alone fail to activate Notch, and how is that block overcome?
cards.back: A folded lock outside the membrane hides Notch's cutting site; mechanical pulling by the sending cell's endocytosis peels the lock open.
cards.quote: In the standard account, the sending cell pulls bound ligand inward by endocytosis (the pinching-in of membrane to form a vesicle), and the tug peels the lock open.
cards.section: Touch, pull and the lock

cards.front: Cultured fly cells that do not normally stick together were made to produce either Notch or Delta and mixed; Notch cells clumped with Delta cells. What does this show?
cards.back: Notch on one cell and Delta on the other interact across cell contacts, so Notch signaling works between touching cells.
cards.quote: In an early test, cultured fly cells that do not normally stick together were made to produce either Notch or Delta, and Notch cells clumped with Delta cells.
cards.section: Touch, pull and the lock

cards.front: Free Notch ligand pieces in solution generally fail to activate Notch cells. What happens if those same ligand pieces are fixed to a culture dish before adding Notch cells, and why?
cards.back: The dish-bound ligand switches Notch on. Fixing the ligand prevents it from drifting with the receptor, creating tension that peels open the negative regulatory region.
cards.quote: Anchoring prevents the ligand from drifting with the receptor, so tension can peel open the negative regulatory region.
cards.section: Touch, pull and the lock

cards.front: What enzyme performs Cut 1 of mammalian Notch, where does it act, and does Cut 1 carry a signal?
cards.back: A furin-like protease cuts Notch's outer part once in the Golgi; the two pieces stay clasped together, preparing Notch without carrying a signal.
cards.quote: The two pieces stay clasped together and reach the surface that way; this cut prepares Notch and carries no signal.
cards.section: One preparation cut and two signal-triggered cuts

cards.front: After the ligand pull exposes Notch's outer cutting site, an {{c1::ADAM}} protease (ADAM10 in mammals) performs Cut 2 and leaves a membrane-anchored stub.
cards.quote: An ADAM protease (ADAM10 in mammals) cuts the newly exposed site. The outer part leaves with the ligand, leaving a membrane-anchored stub.
cards.section: One preparation cut and two signal-triggered cuts

cards.front: Inside the membrane, γ-secretase—a four-protein complex whose cutting subunit is {{c1::presenilin}}—performs Cut 3 to release the Notch intracellular domain.
cards.quote: γ-Secretase—a four-protein complex whose cutting subunit is presenilin—cuts the stub within its membrane-spanning segment.
cards.section: One preparation cut and two signal-triggered cuts

cards.front: Why must extracellular cleavage (Cut 2) occur before γ-secretase can perform intramembrane cleavage (Cut 3) on Notch?
cards.back: γ-Secretase accepts a membrane-anchored stub only after most of Notch's large outer part has been trimmed away.
cards.quote: It accepts a stub only after most of the outer part is trimmed away, so Cut 2 must come first.
cards.section: One preparation cut and two signal-triggered cuts

cards.front: How does presenilin hydrolyze a peptide bond inside an oily lipid bilayer during Notch Cut 3?
cards.back: Presenilin holds its two catalytic aspartates inside a pocket within the membrane that water can reach.
cards.quote: Because hydrolysing a peptide bond needs water in an oily bilayer, presenilin holds its two catalytic aspartates in a pocket water can reach.
cards.section: One preparation cut and two signal-triggered cuts

cards.front: In the standard account, how does the freed Notch intracellular domain (NICD) switch on target genes in the nucleus?
cards.back: NICD binds the DNA-binding protein CSL, displaces co-repressors that hold targets off, and recruits the co-activator Mastermind.
cards.quote: NICD binds CSL, displaces co-repressors and recruits the co-activator Mastermind to switch targets on.
cards.section: One preparation cut and two signal-triggered cuts

cards.front: How does turning on Notch target genes ultimately shut off the nerve-cell fate program?
cards.back: Through a two-step sign flip: Notch activates genes encoding transcriptional repressors (Hes family), which then shut off the nerve program.
cards.quote: Many targets encode Hes-family repressors—a two-step sign flip in which activating a repressor shuts off the nerve programme and tells the cell "not you".
cards.section: One preparation cut and two signal-triggered cuts

cards.front: How does live imaging in flies refine the standard account of CSL binding to DNA when Notch signaling is off?
cards.back: Without signal, CSL binds DNA only briefly rather than remaining stably bound; it stays far longer once NICD and Mastermind arrive.
cards.quote: Live imaging in flies refines the off state: without signal, CSL binds DNA only briefly, staying far longer once NICD and Mastermind arrive.
cards.section: One preparation cut and two signal-triggered cuts

cards.front: A drug selectively inhibits the extracellular protease that performs Cut 2 of Notch, while γ-secretase and ligand pulling remain intact. What happens to nuclear NICD release, and why?
cards.back: No NICD is released to the nucleus. Even when pulling opens the lock, γ-secretase cannot cleave Notch until Cut 2 trims away most of the outer domain.
cards.quote: It accepts a stub only after most of the outer part is trimmed away, so Cut 2 must come first.
cards.section: One preparation cut and two signal-triggered cuts

cards.front: Expressing only the free intracellular domain of Notch activates Notch target fates without any ligand. What does this show, and what objection remains?
cards.back: It shows the inner domain alone carries the signal, but leaves the objection that excess free fragment might drift into nuclei without genuine cleavage of intact receptor.
cards.quote: leaving the objection that excess free fragment might drift into nuclei without real cutting.
cards.section: How proteolytic release was shown

cards.front: Cells make outer-deleted, membrane-anchored Notch1. Normally a shortened fragment enters the nucleus and turns on a reporter; a protease inhibitor keeps Notch uncut at the membrane and turns the reporter off, whereas adding free inner domain restores the reporter. What does this show?
cards.back: Proteolytic cutting is required to release the inner domain from its membrane anchor so it can reach the nucleus and turn on target genes.
cards.quote: In 1996, Raphael Kopan, Eric Schroeter, Harold Weintraub and Jeffrey Nye tested outer-deleted, membrane-anchored mouse Notch1 with and without protease inhibitors.
cards.section: How proteolytic release was shown

cards.front: Struhl and Adachi inserted a transcription activator into the inner tail of intact, full-length Notch in living flies so a sensitive reporter turned on only if the tail reached the nucleus. Where did the reporter turn on, and why?
cards.back: Only where ligand was present. Without a neighbor's ligand, intact Notch stays uncut at the membrane and keeps the activator out of the nucleus.
cards.quote: Without a neighbour's ligand, the intact receptor stays uncut at the membrane and keeps the activator out of the nucleus.
cards.section: How proteolytic release was shown

cards.front: After ligand-induced cleavage of full-length Notch was shown, what did loss-of-Presenilin experiments in flies and mice establish?
cards.back: They showed that Notch signaling and nuclear access of the freed inner domain specifically require Presenilin.
cards.quote: in 1999 Struhl and Greenwald—alongside other fly and mouse laboratories—showed that Notch needs Presenilin to signal.
cards.section: How proteolytic release was shown

cards.front: Why could neither free-tail expression nor outer-deleted membrane-anchored Notch alone prove that ligand triggers cleavage of intact Notch in vivo?
cards.back: Free-tail expression bypasses cutting, and outer-deleted Notch lacks the lock so it cuts without ligand. By the rule that the lock hides the site until ligand pulls—and because endogenous nuclear NICD is too scarce for antibody staining—proving physiological release required intact Notch carrying a sensitive nuclear-access reporter.
cards.quote: Still, endogenous nuclear NICD from intact Notch is too scarce to see by antibody staining.
cards.section: How proteolytic release was shown

cards.front: How does Notch differ from the STAT and Smad pathways in amplification and receptor reuse, even though all three send a protein from membrane to nucleus?
cards.back: STAT/Smad receptors (or borrowed kinases) catalytically modify many copies and are reused; each Notch receptor is irreversibly consumed once to release one NICD without amplification.
cards.quote: There too a protein moves from membrane to nucleus, yet the receptor (or its borrowed kinase) acts catalytically on one STAT or Smad after another.
cards.section: What this design gives up, and what it buys

cards.front: In a signaling cell, 250 Notch receptors are pulled and cut, while 250 active receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) each drive a 20-fold downstream cascade. How many NICDs are released, how many of those 250 Notch receptors remain intact, and how many modified kinase substrates are made?
cards.back: 250 NICDs released, 0 of those 250 Notch receptors left intact, and 5,000 modified substrates (250 × 20), while all 250 RTKs remain intact.
cards.why: Notch has 1:1 irreversible release (250 × 1 = 250) with receptor consumption; a 20-fold catalytic cascade yields 250 × 20 = 5,000 substrates without consuming the RTKs.
cards.quote: 100 pulled Notch receptors release 100 NICDs and leave 100 fewer intact receptors
cards.section: What this design gives up, and what it buys

cards.front: A cell displays 6,000 Notch receptors and neighbors pull on 5% of them in one hour (every pulled Notch is cut). In the same hour, 150 active RTKs each produce 40 phosphorylated downstream molecules. What is the ratio of phosphorylated downstream molecules to released NICDs?
cards.back: 20:1 (6,000 phosphorylated molecules to 300 NICDs). Setup: 5% of 6,000 = 300 pulled Notch → 300 NICDs (1:1); 150 × 40 = 6,000 phosphorylated molecules; 6,000 / 300 = 20.
cards.quote: whereas 100 active receptor kinases driving a 20-fold cascade produce 2,000 modified substrates while all 100 receptors stay intact.
cards.section: What this design gives up, and what it buys

cards.front: What does a cell buy by giving up catalytic amplification and receptor reuse in the Notch pathway?
cards.back: A local, non-diffusing, brief count of direct signaling contacts.
cards.quote: What the cell buys is a local, non-diffusing count.
cards.section: What this design gives up, and what it buys

cards.front: Why does a Notch signal go quiet soon after receptor cutting stops, and what two processes set standing nuclear NICD levels?
cards.back: A nuclear kinase marks NICD's tail, an E3 ligase adds ubiquitin, and the proteasome destroys it; standing nuclear NICD reflects both 1:1 release and rapid clearance.
cards.quote: a nuclear kinase marks NICD's tail, an E3 ligase adds ubiquitin, and the proteasome destroys it
cards.section: What this design gives up, and what it buys

cards.front: A fruit fly with one broken copy of Notch makes roughly half the normal number of receptors. Why does a 50% drop readily cause nicked wings here, unlike in many kinase cascades?
cards.back: Half the receptors yield roughly half the NICD count. With no amplification before the gene to cover the shortfall, a 50% drop readily alters gene output—a likely reason one broken copy nicks the wing.
cards.quote: With no amplification before the gene to cover a shortfall, half the receptors yield roughly half the NICD count—a likely reason one broken Notch copy nicks the wing.
cards.section: What this design gives up, and what it buys

cards.front: In a normal worm larva's gonad, what two fates do the equivalent neighboring cells Z1.ppp and Z4.aaa adopt, and how often does each take the anchor-cell fate?
cards.back: One becomes the anchor cell (AC) and the other a ventral uterine precursor (VU); each takes the AC fate in about half of animals.
cards.quote: Normally one becomes the anchor cell (AC) and the other a ventral uterine precursor (VU), each taking the AC fate in about half of animals.
cards.section: Two equal neighbours, two fates

cards.front: Before diverging into receptor-only VU and ligand-only AC, both equivalent worm gonad cells initially express LIN-12 and its ligand {{c1::LAG-2}}.
cards.quote: both cells initially express LIN-12 and its ligand LAG-2 before diverging into receptor-only VU and ligand-only AC.
cards.section: Two equal neighbours, two fates

cards.front: In the worm larva gonad, killing one of the two equivalent cells with a laser makes the survivor become the anchor cell (AC) in every animal; in mosaics where only cell A lacks the LIN-12 receptor, cell A always becomes the AC and cell B becomes VU. What do these results show?
cards.back: AC is the default fate, whereas the VU fate requires a LIN-12 signal from a neighbor; the cell that cannot hear the signal always ends up as the sender.
cards.quote: The sharpest genetic test comes from a worm larva's gonad, where two equivalent neighbouring cells (Z1.ppp and Z4.aaa) lie side by side.
cards.section: Two equal neighbours, two fates

cards.front: If a mutation locks LIN-12 constitutively ON in both equivalent worm gonad cells without any ligand, what fate do the two cells adopt, and why?
cards.back: Neither becomes an anchor cell. Constitutive LIN-12 runs the received-signal program in both cells, suppressing the default AC fate.
cards.quote: Constitutive LIN-12 runs the received-signal programme in both cells, suppressing the default AC fate.
cards.section: Two equal neighbours, two fates

cards.front: How do cells on a fruit fly's back use contact-dependent Notch signaling to space bristles across several cell diameters?
cards.back: They contact neighbors a few diameters away using thin moving extensions; live imaging shows these help space bristles by allowing local Notch comparison beyond immediate touching neighbors.
cards.quote: including neighbours a few diameters away reached by thin moving extensions on the fly's back (live imaging shows these help space bristles).
cards.section: Two equal neighbours, two fates

cards.front: How does a lateral-inhibition circuit split two identical touching cells into opposite nerve and skin fates without an external cue?
cards.back: Resting on the two lateral-inhibition rules—received signal blocks the nerve program and lowers the cell's own ligand production—a small chance lead in cell A lowers cell B's ligand, which lowers the signal back to A. Two inhibitions in a row create positive feedback across the two cells until A sends (nerve) and B receives (skin).
cards.quote: A slight chance lead in cell A lowers cell B's ligand, which lowers the signal back to A—two inhibitions in a row create positive feedback
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a sheet of identical cells choosing between nerve and skin by lateral inhibition, one mutant cell makes no ligand (Delta) but has normal Notch receptors, while its neighbors are normal. What fate does the mutant cell adopt, and why?
cards.back: It becomes a skin cell. By the two lateral-inhibition rules (received Notch blocks the nerve program and lowers ligand production), its normal neighbors still signal to its Notch receptor and push it toward skin.
cards.quote: Give each cell a surface ligand and a receptor with two rules: received signal blocks the nerve programme (favouring skin) and lowers the cell's own ligand production.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, what are the two main classes of activating NOTCH1 mutations, and how does each increase signaling?
cards.back: One loosens the lock near the membrane so Cut 2 occurs without a pull; the other removes the tail region marking NICD for destruction so each NICD lasts longer.
cards.quote: some loosen the lock near the membrane so Cut 2 happens without a pull, while others remove the tail region that marks NICD for destruction so each NICD lasts longer.
cards.section: When Notch is stuck on, or missing

cards.front: Two T-cell leukaemia lines both have overactive NOTCH1: Line 1 has a lock-loosening mutation, while Line 2 has an intact lock plus a deleted NICD destruction tail. If you block ligand binding outside both lines, how do their responses differ?
cards.back: Line 1 keeps cutting Notch without any pull, whereas Line 2 stops releasing new NICD though existing NICD clears more slowly. This rests on combining the lock rule (an intact lock still requires a ligand pull for Cut 2) with the clearance rule (tail deletion slows proteasomal destruction of already-released NICD).
cards.quote: Patient 2's cells stop releasing new NICD because their intact lock still needs a pull, though existing NICD clears more slowly than normal.
cards.section: When Notch is stuck on, or missing

cards.front: {{c1::Alagille syndrome}} is a dominant genetic disease usually caused by one broken copy of JAG1 (encoding Jagged1), producing too few liver bile ducts and often a heart defect.
cards.quote: Alagille syndrome is a dominant genetic disease in which, in most cases, one copy of JAG1 (encoding Jagged1) is broken.
cards.section: When Notch is stuck on, or missing

cards.front: Why does breaking just one copy of human JAG1 (Alagille syndrome) or fly Notch produce a dominant disease or wing defect, whereas many kinase cascades tolerate a 50% drop?
cards.back: By the rule that Notch is unamplified (1 cut yields 1 NICD with no downstream amplification to buffer a shortfall), half the receptors yield roughly half the NICD, a likely reason one broken Notch copy nicks the wing; as with the fly wing, one working JAG1 copy is not enough in Alagille syndrome.
cards.quote: As in the fly's wing, one working copy is not enough.
cards.section: When Notch is stuck on, or missing

cards.front: Why do γ-secretase inhibitors developed for Alzheimer's disease also block Notch, causing Notch-loss changes such as excess mucus-secreting goblet cells in the rodent gut?
cards.back: γ-Secretase is a shared protease that cuts both amyloid precursor protein and Notch, so blocking it lowers amyloid peptide but also blocks Notch Cut 3.
cards.quote: Drugs that block γ-secretase lower that peptide but also block the Notch cut
cards.section: When Notch is stuck on, or missing

cards.front: Suppose you treat two overactive-Notch cell lines—Line 1 (lock-loosening mutation) and Line 2 (intact lock plus deleted NICD destruction tail)—with a γ-secretase inhibitor instead of a ligand blocker. What happens to new NICD release in each line, and what tissue risk arises?
cards.back: New NICD release stops in both lines, while blocking γ-secretase risks Notch-loss defects in normal tissues such as the gut lining. This rests on two rules: intramembrane cleavage (Cut 3) by γ-secretase is downstream of the lock and required to release NICD from any membrane-anchored Notch, and γ-secretase is shared across tissues.
cards.quote: Drugs that block γ-secretase lower that peptide but also block the Notch cut
cards.section: When Notch is stuck on, or missing

cards.front: What shared structural feature united fruit fly Notch and worm LIN-12 into one receptor family?
cards.back: Both are large single-pass membrane proteins whose outer parts carry repeats resembling epidermal growth factor (36 in fly Notch).
cards.quote: finding a large single-pass membrane protein with 36 outer repeats resembling epidermal growth factor.
cards.section: How fly Notch and worm lin-12 were linked (1985)
